metadata.title: Modeling mathematics achievement with deep learning methods
metadata.venue: Sigma Journal of Engineering and Natural Sciences

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses Turkey’s PISA 2018 survey data and builds a classification model for mathematics achievement success vs. failure using student questionnaire variables (e.g., gender, ESCS, home possessions, ICT resources). The manuscript does not report whether complex survey sampling weights or replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any PISA weight variables (e.g., student weights) or describe variance estimation under the PISA design. Because the models are deep learning and neural-network classifiers (Elman/Jordan neural networks, MLP) and logistic regression/MLP baselines, the paper does not indicate any weight-aware training or weighted loss. Therefore, readers should treat the reported predictive performance as based on the authors’ analytic sample without documented complex-survey weighting adjustments.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is PV1MATH (Mathematical Achievement), but the paper does not describe how missing values in predictors or the PV outcome were handled (e.g., whether cases with missing questionnaire responses were excluded or imputed). This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain non-trivial missingness in background variables, and the choice of deletion vs. imputation can affect model training and evaluation. The paper also does not specify whether PV1MATH was used as a single draw consistently across the modeling pipeline, beyond listing PV1MATH as the achievement feature.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses Turkey’s PISA 2018 data and constructs the target by selecting the most successful 30% and the most unsuccessful 30% of students (a 60% subset) for mathematics achievement classification. The paper does not report additional grade-level restrictions, item-level exclusions, or missing-data exclusions beyond this success/failure selection. The analytic sample is therefore defined primarily by the top/bottom 30% achievement grouping using PV1MATH.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Jordan neural network (test): Accuracy=0.826, AUC=0.739; also reported (test) Error Rate=0.174, Sensitivity=0.826, Specificity=0.869, False Positive Rate=0.131, F1-Score=0.826.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Turkey the study leveraged Gender, Sense of school belonging, Socioeconomic status (ESCS), Home possessions, and Parents’ emotional support to predict Mathematics achievement success vs. failure (top/bottom 30%), finding that the Jordan neural network achieved the highest test accuracy (0.826) and AUC (0.739) among the compared models. This indicates that deep learning models can effectively classify students’ mathematics success using readily available student background and home/ICT factors, suggesting that education systems could use such models for targeted support—while noting that the paper does not document survey-weighting or missing-data handling and therefore causality cannot be inferred.

data.outcome_summary: The study models mathematics achievement success vs. failure using Turkey’s PISA 2018 data, defining the target by selecting the most successful 30% and the most unsuccessful 30% of students based on PV1MATH. It compares deep learning classifiers (Elman neural network, Jordan neural network) with a multilayer perceptron and logistic regression, evaluating performance on training and test splits using Accuracy, Error Rate, Sensitivity, Specificity, False Positive Rate, F1-Score, and ROC/AUC. On the test set, the Jordan neural network is the best-performing model with Accuracy=0.826 and AUC=0.739 (also Sensitivity=0.826, Specificity=0.869, F1-Score=0.826). The paper reports that gender, sense of belonging, socioeconomic status, household items, emotional support, ICT devices at home, and digital device use in lessons were effective predictors. Limitations include lack of documented complex-survey weighting and missing-data handling, and the use of predictive classification rather than causal identification.
